435.title: Out of the depths (Psalm 130)
435.hook: my soul waits more than watchmen for the morning
435.howItsDone: Psalm 130 is one of the seven penitential psalms; Catholics traditionally pray the De profundis for the dead, many churches sing it at evening prayer and funerals, and Lutherans sing Luther's hymn version.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dreamers, and a farmer planting through tears. Your line was sow in tears, reap in joy. What small hopeful thing did you plant? Day four hundred thirty-five.

Four in the morning on a city wall. The watchman has been up since midnight. His eyes ache. The torches are low. Every shadow in the valley could be an enemy, and it's his job to see it first. Nothing to do but stand there and look east. He knows morning will come. It always has. But knowing doesn't make the last hour shorter. He watches the sky for the first thin gray line along the hills, the sign that he can finally go home and sleep. Anyone who has worked a night shift, sat up with a sick child, or waited for a phone call knows that hour. Today's psalm lives there.
screen: `FOUR A.M. ON THE WALL.` → `EYES ON THE EAST.` → `THE LONGEST HOUR.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred thirty is short, eight verses, and it begins at the bottom. In the King James Bible: "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD." Depths is the word for deep water, the kind you go under. In Latin the psalm is known by its first words, De profundis. Then comes a startling question: "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?" If God kept a record of every wrong, nobody would be left on their feet. The answer comes straight away: "But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared." Not a God with a ledger. A God with forgiveness, which makes him worth revering. Then the waiting. "I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope. My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning." He says it twice. You can feel the hour dragging. And then, in the last two verses, the psalmist turns from himself to his whole people: let Israel hope, for with the Lord there is mercy, and plenteous redemption. Christians have long counted this among the seven penitential psalms, prayers of turning back. Martin Luther made it a hymn. Catholics pray the De profundis for the dead, and it is sung at evening prayer. It's also another song of going up, from the pilgrims' collection. Which means the people who sang it out of the depths were walking uphill as they sang.
screen: `DE PROFUNDIS: OUT OF THE DEPTHS` · `NOT A LEDGER, BUT FORGIVENESS` · `MORE THAN WATCHMEN FOR MORNING` · `FROM ONE VOICE TO A PEOPLE` · then, large: `MY SOUL WAITETH FOR THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait for one thing with hope. Sit, and let your body settle. Name to yourself one thing you're waiting for. A result, a reconciliation, a change in someone you love, a morning after a long night. Hold it the way the watchman holds the horizon: not grabbing, not giving up. Eyes on the east. Breathe slowly. Each breath out is one more minute closer to the light. If you pray, you can say: my soul waiteth for the Lord. If you don't, simply wait, hoping, without demanding when. The bell holds the time.
De profundis. Latin for out of the depths, Psalm one hundred thirty's cry from deep water, and a soul waiting for God more than watchmen wait for morning.
Your line: more than watchmen for morning. Today, if you're waiting on something hard, watch for one first sign of light, however small, and name it when it comes. Day four hundred thirty-five.

436.title: A weaned child (Psalm 131)
436.hook: I've calmed and quieted my soul like a weaned child with its mother
436.howItsDone: Christians in contemplative traditions often pray Psalm 131 before silent prayer, and it is sung at evening prayer in many churches and monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a cry out of the depths, and a soul waiting more than watchmen for morning. Did you catch a first sign of light? Day four hundred thirty-six.

Watch a nursing baby on a parent's lap. All need. Rooting, fussing, grabbing, turning toward the one thing it wants, crying until it gets it. Nothing wrong with that; that's what babies are for. Now watch an older child on the same lap. Weaned. Not hungry, not asking for anything. Just leaning back against a parent's chest, legs dangling, watching the room. Heavy and calm. There because it's a good place to be, and for no other reason. Same lap, same parent, a completely different way of being held. A psalm only three verses long is about that difference.
screen: `A NURSING BABY: ALL NEED.` → `A WEANED CHILD: JUST LEANING.` → `THE SAME LAP.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred thirty-one is three verses long. Here's the first, in the King James Bible: "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me." Haughty means lifted up. Lofty eyes are eyes always looking above their station. And exercise myself means busy myself, chase after. The writer has stopped straining after things too big to grasp. Not because they don't matter, but because they're not his to carry. Then verse two: "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child." In the book of Samuel, Hannah keeps her boy at home until he's weaned, and only then brings him to the temple. So a weaned child isn't a newborn. It's a small person who no longer needs the breast, and yet still climbs into its mother's lap. That's the picture of the soul here. Not empty of desire. Quieted. With God, not to get something, just to be there. The writer says he did this himself: I have behaved and quieted myself. It took effort to get still. Then the last verse turns outward again, like Psalm one hundred thirty did: "Let Israel hope in the LORD from henceforth and for ever." It's another song of going up, and the heading gives it to David. Some Christian contemplatives use this little psalm as a picture of prayer that asks for nothing.
screen: `NOT HAUGHTY, NOT LOFTY` · `THINGS TOO HIGH FOR ME` · `WEANED: NOT HUNGRY, STILL HELD` · `I HAVE QUIETED MYSELF` · then, large: `MY SOUL IS EVEN AS A WEANED CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest without asking for anything. For these two minutes, set down every request. No list. No fixing. No improving yourself. If something you want comes to mind, notice it, and let it go by. Let your back be supported by the chair, the way a child leans against a parent. Let your breathing be heavy and slow. If you pray, you can simply rest in God's presence, wordless, like the child in the lap. If you don't, just rest, asking nothing of the minute. The bell holds the time.
A weaned child. Psalm one hundred thirty-one's picture of a quiet soul: not hungry, not grabbing, simply leaning on the one who holds it.
Your line: quieted, like a child. Today, find one moment to stop striving at something too high for you, and just lean back. Day four hundred thirty-six.

437.title: By the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137)
437.hook: exiles weep and hang up their harps; the psalm even holds their rage honestly
437.howItsDone: Christians pray Psalm 137 in times of exile, grief and injustice; some churches omit its final verses in public worship, while others pray it whole as an honest lament.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a weaned child leaning on its mother. Your line was quieted, like a child. Did you stop striving long enough to lean back? Day four hundred thirty-seven.

A reggae song built from this psalm, and later a disco version, put it on dance floors. People dance to it at weddings and roller rinks, singing about sitting down by the rivers of Babylon. The words are far older than the beat, and the psalm ends somewhere no party goes. Go back to the days after the fall of Jerusalem. The Babylonian army has burned the city and its temple. Its people have been marched east, far from home, to the rivers and canals of Babylon. And their captors, in a cruel joke, ask them to sing.
screen: `A SONG ON THE DANCE FLOOR.` → `JERUSALEM IN FLAMES.` → `SING US A SONG OF ZION.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof." Then the cruelty: "For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion." Entertain us with your homeland's songs. And the answer is the question at the center of the psalm: "How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?" They won't perform their grief for the people who caused it. Then a vow: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." Cunning means skill. A harpist's right hand. Let me never play again if I forget home. Now the hard part. The last three verses turn to rage. They call down judgment on Edom, which cheered the destruction, and on Babylon, and the very last verse blesses whoever would dash Babylon's little ones against the stones. It is hard to hear. And it's in the Bible. Christians have handled it in different ways. Some churches leave those verses out when the psalm is prayed aloud. Augustine and other early writers read the little ones as small evil thoughts, to be dashed against the rock, which they took to be Christ. Other readers see the psalm as honest rage handed over to God in words, instead of acted out in the world. What the psalm doesn't do is pretend. The Bible keeps the tears, the vow and the fury of people who lost everything.
screen: `HARPS HUNG ON THE WILLOWS` · `SING US ONE OF THE SONGS OF ZION` · `IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM` · `RAGE KEPT IN THE TEXT, HONESTLY` · then, large: `HOW SHALL WE SING THE LORD'S SONG IN A STRANGE LAND?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for people far from home. Sit, and breathe. Think of people who are where they never chose to be. Refugees in camps. Families split across borders. Someone in a hospital far from their town. A neighbor who moved here and still cooks food that smells like somewhere else. Picture one face, if you can. If you pray, you can hold them before God, by name or simply as they are. If you don't, hold them in mind with care, and let yourself feel a little of what they've lost. The bell holds the time.
By the rivers of Babylon. Psalm one hundred thirty-seven: exiles who hang up their harps, refuse to sing for their captors, and keep their rage honest.
screen: `BY THE RIVERS OF BABYLON — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: how can we sing here? Today, if you meet someone far from home, ask them one question about where they come from, and really listen to the answer. Day four hundred thirty-seven.

438.title: You knit me together (Psalm 139)
438.hook: you know when I sit and rise; if I take the wings of morning, you are there
438.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 139 as a prayer of being known by God; its last verses, "Search me, O God," are often prayed before confession or at the end of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, by the rivers of Babylon, harps hung on the willows. Your line was how can we sing here? Who did you think of, far from home? Day four hundred thirty-eight.

On a lot of refrigerators there's a small, grainy, black-and-white picture held up by a magnet. You have to squint. A curve that might be a spine. A blur that might be a hand. The people who put it there can tell you exactly which smudge is the nose. Before anyone has held this child, before anyone knows its laugh, it is already known, already loved, already the picture everyone stops to look at. Long before ultrasound, a psalm imagined that same hidden beginning, and claimed that someone was watching it closely. Today, Psalm one hundred thirty-nine, the psalm of being known all the way down.
screen: `A GRAINY PICTURE ON THE FRIDGE.` → `KNOWN BEFORE BEING HELD.` → `KNOWN ALL THE WAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: It begins, in the King James Bible: "O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off." Sitting down, getting up, a thought before it's finished. Then the writer tries to imagine getting away. "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?" Up to heaven: you're there. Down to the grave: you're there. "If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me." The wings of the morning: fly as fast as the dawn moves across the sky, all the way to the far edge of the sea. Still held. Then the psalm goes inward, to the womb. The King James says, "thou hast covered me in my mother's womb." The Hebrew verb can mean cover, or weave together, which is why many later translations say knit. Two verses on, the writer says he was "curiously wrought" in secret, a phrase for embroidery, colored thread worked by hand. And in between, the line: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Fearfully here means with awe, the way you'd handle something precious. Then the psalm surprises. Near the end, the psalm turns angry: the writer wants God to slay the wicked. And then, right after, he stops and turns the searchlight on himself: "Search me, O God, and know my heart." See if there's any wicked way in me. A psalm that starts with being searched ends by asking for it.
screen: `MY DOWNSITTING AND MINE UPRISING` · `THE WINGS OF THE MORNING` · `WOVEN, EMBROIDERED IN SECRET` · `SEARCH ME, O GOD` · then, large: `I AM FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: place your hand on your heart. Gently, flat, so you can feel it beating. Close your eyes if you like. This heart started beating before you knew you existed. Somebody, the psalm says, was paying attention even then. Feel the rhythm under your palm. Feel the breath lifting your hand a little, and letting it down. If you pray, you can say the line slowly: I am fearfully and wonderfully made. If you don't, simply feel how carefully you are put together, and let that be enough. The bell holds the time.
You knit me together. Psalm one hundred thirty-nine's picture of a life woven in secret, and known all the way down.
Your line: fearfully and wonderfully made. Today, when you catch yourself criticizing your own body or mind, stop, and handle yourself with a little awe instead. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

439.title: Everything praise (Psalm 148)
439.hook: sun, moon, sea monsters, snow, kings and children, praise
439.carry: a cedar praises by growing like a cedar
439.howItsDone: Psalm 148 is a traditional morning praise psalm in many churches, and it is echoed in the Benedicite canticle and in hymns such as "All Creatures of Our God and King."

segments.voice: Yesterday, a life woven in secret. Your line was fearfully and wonderfully made. Where did your hand rest, and what did you feel there? Day four hundred thirty-nine.

A choir director stands up before the concert and takes the roll. Sopranos? Here. Altos? Here. Tenors, basses? Here. Now keep the roll call going. Angels? Sun and moon? Stars? Here. Sea monsters? Here. Fire, hail, snow, fog, the stormy wind? Here. Mountains, fruit trees, cedars, wild animals, cattle, creeping things, birds? Kings, judges, young men and young women, old people and children? All here. That roll call is Psalm one hundred forty-eight. It doesn't ask who believes, who is important, or who can carry a tune. It calls everything into the choir.
screen: `SOPRANOS? ALTOS?` → `SEA MONSTERS? HAIL?` → `EVERYTHING INTO THE CHOIR.`

segments.voice: The psalm has two halves, like a camera tilting from the sky down to the ground. First, from the heavens: angels, hosts, and then, in the King James Bible, "Praise ye him, sun and moon: praise him, all ye stars of light." Then, from verse seven, the earth: "Praise the LORD from the earth, ye dragons, and all deeps." Dragons. The Hebrew is tanninim, great sea creatures, the same word Genesis uses when God creates the great sea monsters on the fifth day. Creatures that frightened the ancient imagination are in the choir. Then the weather. "Fire, and hail; snow, and vapour; stormy wind fulfilling his word." A storm, in this psalm, isn't chaos. It's doing what it was told. Then mountains and fruit trees, beasts and creeping things, and finally people, every rank mixed together: "Both young men, and maidens; old men, and children." Kings stand in the same row as kids. Why should a rock or a snowflake praise? One old answer: not with words, but by being what it is. A cedar praises by growing like a cedar. The psalm's list has echoes. In the Greek Bible, the book of Daniel includes a long song of three young men in a furnace, calling on everything from frost to whales to bless the Lord; Catholics and Orthodox read it as scripture, and Anglicans sing it as the Benedicite. And Francis of Assisi wrote his Canticle of the Creatures, praising God through Brother Sun and Sister Moon. Today's hymn All Creatures of Our God and King comes from it.
screen: `FROM THE HEAVENS: SUN AND MOON` · `FROM THE EARTH: SEA MONSTERS` · `STORMY WIND FULFILLING HIS WORD` · `KINGS IN THE SAME ROW AS CHILDREN` · then, large: `PRAISE YE THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name ten things in creation. Slowly, one at a time, out loud or in your head. Look around first, then let your mind travel. The light in the window. A cloud. A crow. A tree you pass every day. Rain. Your grandmother's hands. A child somewhere laughing. Something huge, something tiny. Give each one a breath before you move on. When you reach ten, sit with the whole crowd of them. If you pray, you can let each name be a small praise. If you don't, simply let the list be wonder. The bell holds the time.
Everything praise. Psalm one hundred forty-eight's roll call: angels, stars, sea monsters, hail, cedars, kings and children, all called into one choir.
Your line: a cedar praises by growing like a cedar. Today, pick one ordinary thing, the weather, a tree, a puddle, and imagine it singing simply by being itself. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

screen: `DAY 439 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LET EVERYTHING THAT HAS BREATH.`

440.title: Let everything that has breath (Psalm 150)
440.hook: trumpet, harp, cymbals, dance: the psalter ends in pure praise
440.carry: your breath goes back as praise
440.howItsDone: Christians sing hallelujah (or alleluia) throughout worship, especially at Easter; many Western churches set it aside during Lent, while Orthodox Christians sing it all year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a roll call of sea monsters, snow and children. Your line was a cedar praises by growing like a cedar. What ordinary thing did you hear singing? Day four hundred forty.
screen: `A CEDAR PRAISES BY GROWING LIKE A CEDAR.`

segments.voice: You've probably said today's word without thinking about it. Shouted in a gospel choir. Sung by a whole hall standing up in the middle of a Christmas concert. Muttered when the bus finally shows up after twenty minutes in the rain. Typed in all capitals when the exam results come in. It's one of a handful of words that have traveled, nearly unchanged, from ancient Hebrew into dozens of languages around the world. And it's the word the whole book of Psalms ends on. After a hundred and forty-nine psalms of tears, rage, waiting and thanks, the last one has no story and no request. Just instruments, dancing and one word.
screen: `A GOSPEL CHOIR.` → `THE BUS FINALLY COMES.` → `THE LAST WORD OF THE PSALMS.`

segments.voice: Hallelujah is two Hebrew words joined. Hallelu means praise, and it's plural, a command to a crowd: all of you, praise. Yah is a short form of God's own name. So hallelujah means: everybody, praise the Lord. The King James Bible usually translates it instead of spelling it out, which is why Psalm one hundred fifty begins and ends with "Praise ye the LORD." In between, an orchestra. "Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp. Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs. Praise him upon the loud cymbals: praise him upon the high sounding cymbals." The trumpet here is likely the shofar, the ram's horn. The timbrel is a hand drum. And organs isn't a pipe organ. In 1611 the word could mean any musical instrument; the Hebrew probably means a pipe or flute. Loud cymbals and high sounding cymbals: the psalm wants it noisy. Then the last line: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Not everything with a voice, or with faith, or with talent. Everything with breath. The Hebrew word for breath is neshamah, the same word Genesis uses when God breathes into the first human the breath of life. The breath that was given goes back as praise. In the New Testament, the word appears only in Revelation, in Greek as alleluia, sung by a great multitude in heaven. Many Western churches stop saying alleluia during Lent and bring it back with joy at Easter; Orthodox Christians keep singing it all year round.
screen: `HALLELU: ALL OF YOU, PRAISE` · `YAH: THE NAME OF GOD` · `SHOFAR, HARP, DRUM, CYMBALS` · `NESHAMAH: THE BREATH OF LIFE` · then, large: `LET EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH PRAISE THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe out with a word of praise. Sit, and notice your breathing. It came in this morning without you asking. Breathe in slowly, all the way. Then, on the out-breath, let a word ride out with it. If you pray, that word can be hallelujah, said softly, or just a long breath out with the thought of it. If you don't, let the word be thanks, or simply let the breath itself go out as gratitude. In, given. Out, given back. Again, for as long as the bell allows. The bell holds the time.
Hallelujah. Hebrew for: all of you, praise the Lord. The last word of the book of Psalms, and one of the most traveled words on earth.
Your line: your breath goes back as praise. Today, every time you notice yourself breathing, let one breath out be a small thanks. Day four hundred forty.

441.title: Five books of prayers
441.hook: the Psalms are in five books, like the Torah, and cover every feeling
441.howItsDone: Many Christians pray through the whole book of Psalms regularly: monasteries traditionally chant all 150 every week, and the Book of Common Prayer sets them out to be read through every month.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last psalm, all trumpets and cymbals. Your word was hallelujah, and your line, your breath goes back as praise. Did a breath go out as thanks? Day four hundred forty-one.

Open a Bible somewhere near the middle and you may well land in the Psalms: a hundred and fifty of them. For the last month this path has walked through it: a tree by the water, a cry of my God, my God, a deer at a dry stream, a sparrow at the altar, a weaned child, exiles by the rivers of Babylon, and yesterday, a crash of cymbals. It can feel like a shuffle playlist. Grief, then joy, then fury, then a lullaby. But it isn't a pile. Someone arranged it. Today, before we leave the Psalms, the shape of the whole book.
screen: `THE MIDDLE OF THE BIBLE.` → `A MONTH IN THE PSALMS.` → `NOT A PILE, A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: The Psalms are divided into five books. Book one runs from Psalm one to forty-one. Book two, forty-two to seventy-two. Book three, seventy-three to eighty-nine. Book four, ninety to one hundred six. Book five, one hundred seven to one hundred fifty. You can see the seams if you look. The first four books each end with a blessing, like a door closing, and the fifth ends with yesterday's hallelujah. The first one, in the King James Bible: "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen." And at the end of book two there's a surprising little note: "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended." Except they aren't. More psalms of David come later. Some scholars think that line is left over from an older collection, stitched in whole, a sign the book was gathered from earlier collections. An old Jewish commentary on the Psalms says that as Moses gave Israel five books of the law, David gave them five books of psalms. Inside, every feeling has a place. Lament runs all through it: complaint, grief, why, how long. Then praise, thanks, pilgrim songs, wisdom, songs for kings. Early Christian writers noticed this. Athanasius, a bishop of Alexandria, wrote that the other books of the Bible speak to you, but the Psalms speak for you; you find your own soul in them, as in a mirror. John Calvin later called the book an anatomy of all the parts of the soul. One more note: Greek and Latin Bibles number most psalms one lower, which is why Catholic and Orthodox prayer books can look off by one.
screen: `FIVE BOOKS, FIVE SEAMS` · `THE PRAYERS OF DAVID ARE ENDED` · `LAMENT RUNS ALL THROUGH IT` · `A MIRROR FOR THE SOUL` · then, large: `EVERY FEELING HAS A PSALM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose a psalm for this week. Sit for a moment and ask yourself honestly how you are. Tired? Grateful? Angry? Waiting? Homesick? Then think back over this month's psalms and let one rise that fits. The deer at the dry stream. The very present help. Out of the depths. The weaned child. The new song. Don't pick the one you think you should. Pick the one that sounds like you. Hold it in mind for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can pray it this week. If you don't, read it once a day as a mirror. The bell holds the time.
Five books of prayers. The Psalms, gathered into five collections, each ending in a blessing, with room for every feeling.

Your line: every feeling has a psalm. This week we went from the depths to a weaned child, Babylon, being knit together, everything praising, and hallelujah. Today, when a strong feeling comes, ask which psalm has already prayed it. Day four hundred forty-one.

fork.setup: you're editing a book of prayers for a whole people. you have joyful songs, angry songs, sad songs. what do you do with the sad ones?
options: cut them, to keep it uplifting.
put them all at the back.
keep them throughout the book.

original.note: Hebrew: praises. the Hebrew name of the book of Psalms, though it is full of laments.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Psalms are a big hymnbook in no special order.
what it means: five collections, stitched together, with a psalm for every feeling.
what a scholar hears: books one to four end with a doxology (41:13, 72:18–19, 89:52, 106:48), and 72:20 is a seam left from an earlier collection.
